resources.title: Understanding Conflict
resources.summary: How to distinguish productive tension from relationship breakdown, understand conflict escalation levels, identify structural sources of friction, and build a conflict map that diagnoses what is actually happening.

sections.heading: What this resource is for
sections.text: In AI-accelerated organisations, the pace of individual and team output increases, and so does the surface area for friction. More work in motion means more dependencies, more decisions, and more opportunities for misalignment between people and teams. Not all of that friction is conflict, but some of it is, and knowing the difference matters. Conflicts are a natural and normal part of everyday life. They form in close relationships, in workplaces, communities, and even on an international level. As inevitable as they are, the outcome does not have to be negative. Conflicts can challenge us to think harder, be more creative, develop greater understanding, and search for more efficient, more effective, and more productive approaches. To harness that potential, we have to learn to handle them constructively. Unresolved conflict, however, can result in the breakdown of a group. In the workplace, unaddressed conflict reduces morale, hampers performance, and increases absences. It leads to increased stress, decreased productivity, and — at worst — open hostility. Conflict mapping is a diagnostic practice that helps you see what kind of conflict you are actually dealing with before you try to resolve it. Getting the diagnosis right is the most important step: the wrong intervention applied to the wrong conflict type makes things worse, not better.

sections.heading: Disagreements vs. conflicts
sections.text: The big difference between disagreements and conflicts is that two people having a disagreement can remain good friends or colleagues — their relationship stays intact and contact is upheld. In conflicts, relationships turn sour and communication ends. Conflicts are disagreements that lead to tension within and between people. The disagreement concerns an issue, whereas the ensuing tension affects the relationship. A conflict therefore always has a dual character: it involves both an issue and a relationship. Effective conflict resolution must address both. If you do not deal with the issue at hand, solutions will be short-lived. If you do not deal with the affected relationship, tension between those in conflict will remain.

sections.heading: The core distinction: productive tension vs. relationship breakdown
sections.text: Not all conflict is harmful. Organisations that avoid all disagreement tend to make poor decisions, because important trade-offs never get surfaced. The goal is not to eliminate conflict but to distinguish conflict that generates value from conflict that consumes it. Productive tension is disagreement about ideas, priorities, approaches, or trade-offs. It is task-focused. The people involved may be frustrated or at odds, but the underlying relationship is intact. This kind of conflict is worth facilitating, not suppressing — the discomfort it creates is a signal that something real and important is being worked through. Relationship breakdown is conflict that has shifted from the task to the person. One or both parties have formed a negative model of the other's character or intent. Trust has eroded. Communication has become guarded or adversarial. This is not a disagreement you can resolve by clarifying requirements or redesigning a process, it requires a different intervention focused on restoring psychological safety and rebuilding a working relationship. The practical test: ask yourself whether, if you removed the work topic entirely, the two people would still be in friction. If yes, the conflict has moved into relationship territory.

sections.heading: The five dimensions of conflict
sections.text: Conflict arises from a clash of perceptions, goals, or values in a domain where people care about the outcome. When it comes to conflict, various differences may be at play: people may differ on what the problem is, have different perspectives on the same problem, or share the same perspective but have different ideas about the solution. Understanding which dimension a conflict is rooted in helps determine what kind of intervention is most likely to work. Most conflicts span more than one dimension. The structural dimension is the external framework people live and work within: legislation, ownership, and organisational structure. Conflicts rooted here cannot be resolved directly through interpersonal work, the structure itself needs attention. Dealing with a specific conflict may, however, illuminate structural issues that need to change to prevent future ones. The instrumental dimension is where two parties disagree about how a given task should be handled. These conflicts are often quite concrete and tend to stay focused on the issue rather than escalating to the person. They can usually be approached through argumentation and finding solutions both parties find acceptable. The dimension of interest is centred on resources: money, time, space, influence, or power. When resources are scarce, people compete. Conflicts in this dimension are best approached through negotiation to reach agreement on the distribution of what is contested. The dimension of value concerns personal and cultural values — ideology, moral principles, professional ethics. These are things people are willing to fight for. Conflicts rooted in values are among the hardest to resolve because values are not negotiable in the way interests are. The goal here is not to change values but to reach a greater understanding of the other party's position. Open dialogue, appreciative inquiry, and non-violent communication are the appropriate tools . The personal dimension is where people are driven by strong emotions and fears: questions of identity, recognition, loyalty, rejection, and self-esteem. "Do people recognise my worth?" "Am I being left out?" Conflicts that have reached this dimension are among the most intense, because they touch what people care most deeply about. As with value conflicts, open dialogue and non-violent communication are the appropriate approaches. An analysis of the dimensions of a conflict provides knowledge about where to begin and where to focus energy when attempting to address it.

sections.heading: How conflicts escalate
sections.text: When conflicts develop unhindered, or when those involved continue to fuel them, they escalate through predictable stages. As escalation progresses, the original issue becomes more and more obscured, and what becomes important is how wrong the other person is. Communication ends. Only the negative relationship remains. Level 1 — Disagreement : "We just don't want the same thing." At this stage there is no real conflict, merely a difference of opinion. Both parties attempt, reasonably, to find a solution. Things may not be resolved, however, and someone crosses a professional or personal boundary. The other party reacts, and the situation escalates. Level 2 — Personification : "It's your fault." Focus shifts from the issue to the persons involved. Negative emotions such as fear and confusion begin to interfere with communication. Doubts about the other party's intentions arise and make it difficult to think clearly about the original issue. Level 3 — The problem expands : "This is not the first time they have done this!" Old discrepancies that have nothing to do with the original issue are brought in. Things thought long forgotten are suddenly remembered. At this level, dialogue stops and the relationship is severed — not just temporarily, but potentially for good. Maintaining some kind of contact, however difficult, is of paramount importance if resolution is to remain possible. Level 4 — Alliance building : "Let the gossip start." Negative feelings narrow thought patterns. Communication becomes imprecise and both parties distort what the other is saying. Selective hearing is prevalent. People seek out allies who confirm their position and validate their view of the other party's failings. Level 5 — Enemy images : "They're no good." As contact and communication with the other party ends, one becomes entrenched in increasingly fixed views of the other. It becomes difficult to find any redeeming qualities in them at all. Level 6 — Open hostility : "It's them or us." The other party is no longer viewed with basic good faith. Open hostility — psychological or physical — becomes possible. The sentiment "the ends justify the means" appears. Voices of moderation are shunned as naïve or unreliable. Level 7 — Separation : "Let's get away." Co-existence is no longer seen as possible. The practical question for most workplace conflicts is: what level is this at, and which direction is it moving? Levels 1–2 can often be addressed through facilitated conversation about the substance. By Level 3, the relationship dimension requires attention before any substantive work can happen. By Levels 4–5, de-escalation and possibly mediation are necessary first steps.

sections.heading: Responses to conflict: flight, fight, and openness
sections.text: When faced with conflict, people typically respond in one of three ways. Flight can manifest as evasiveness, ignoring the issue, denial, belittling the problem, or physically or emotionally withdrawing from contact with the other person. Fight manifests as retaliation, sarcasm, psychological or physical aggression, or condescending and patronising behaviour. Openness means recognising that a conflict exists and that you are part of it, being willing to maintain contact, and engaging in dialogue with genuine curiosity about the other person's perspective. These are not moral categories, there are situations where each response is sensible and relevant. Experience shows, however, that when it is possible to choose, openness tends to produce the most durable outcomes.

sections.heading: Common structural sources of conflict
sections.text: Before assuming a conflict is interpersonal, check for structural causes. These are the most common ones in software and product organisations. Ownership ambiguity occurs when two teams or individuals both believe they are responsible for something, or both believe they are not. This creates either damaging overlap or a vacuum. The conflict that surfaces between people is real, but the root cause is a structural gap that no amount of interpersonal skill will fix. Competing incentives occur when two people or teams are each optimising rationally for their own goals, and those goals are in tension. A feature team optimising for delivery speed and a platform team optimising for stability will generate recurring friction — not because either is wrong, but because their success criteria pull in different directions. This conflict is best resolved at the level of goal design, not individual behaviour. Information asymmetry occurs when one party has context the other lacks, leading to decisions or behaviours that seem irrational or hostile from the outside. Much apparent stubbornness dissolves when the missing information is shared. Dependency without coordination is a structural condition common in AI-accelerated environments, where teams move faster than their coordination mechanisms can keep up with . Conflicts that look interpersonal are often this structure breaking down.

sections.heading: How to map a conflict
sections.text: A conflict map is a structured representation of a tension in your organisation. The value is in making implicit things explicit so they can be examined together. Step 1: Name the parties. Who is in this conflict? Be specific — name individuals or teams, not vague groupings. Step 2: State the surface issue. What is the disagreement about, in concrete terms? This is what people would say if you asked them what the problem is. Step 3: Identify the dimensions. Using the five dimensions above, where does this conflict appear to be rooted? Is it instrumental — a concrete disagreement about how something should be done? Or does it run into interests, values, or the personal dimension? This determines what kind of intervention has any chance of working. Step 4: Surface the underlying needs. Behind every stated position is an underlying need or concern . A team that "refuses to adopt the new tooling" may actually be concerned about delivery risk, or about not being consulted. Identifying underlying needs opens up solution space that negotiating on positions closes down. Step 5: Identify structural contributors. What in the organisation's structure, incentives, or processes is feeding this conflict? Would this conflict exist if the structure were different? Step 6: Assess the escalation level. Using the seven-level model above, where is this conflict right now? What level is it at, and which direction is it moving? Step 7: Identify the right intervention. A conflict at Level 1–2 in the instrumental dimension with a structural cause may need a process design intervention, not a conversation. A conflict at Level 3+ with relationship damage needs facilitated dialogue before anything structural can be addressed.

resources.title: Constructive Disagreement and Feedback
resources.summary: Why feedback conversations fail and how to avoid the common failure modes. The SARA model: understanding the emotional arc of receiving difficult feedback. Non-violent communication: observations, feelings, needs, and requests. A practical structure for delivering and receiving feedback.

sections.heading: What this resource is for
sections.text: As AI accelerates delivery, the conversations that were already uncomfortable become more frequent and more consequential. Misalignment that previously had weeks to surface now needs to be caught in days. Feedback that was deferred indefinitely now has a real cost. The skills covered in this resource — giving and receiving feedback, having difficult conversations constructively — are not soft skills in an AI-accelerated environment. They are coordination infrastructure. Knowing that a conflict exists and understanding its structure is necessary but not sufficient. At some point, someone has to have the conversation. This resource covers the skills and models that make difficult feedback conversations productive: understanding the emotional arc of receiving hard news, structuring feedback so it is heard rather than defended against, and communicating in a way that preserves the relationship while still addressing the substance.

sections.heading: Why feedback matters and why it is difficult
sections.text: Feedback is essential for growth as a person, a team, a product, or an organisation. It is not always easy to accept, however. When you are not used to receiving feedback, it can make you feel uncomfortable. Feedback can hurt, especially when it is interpreted as a critique of your person rather than a suggestion for improvement. This can lead people to avoid feedback or reject it even when it would genuinely help them. Feedback comes in many forms: performance conversations, peer observations, mentoring, retrospectives, or even a failed project that signals something about how the work is being done. What all useful feedback has in common is that it is actionable, specific, and aimed at behaviour rather than character. Most people give feedback with positive intent — they want the other person to succeed. That intent does not automatically make the feedback well-delivered, well-timed, or well-received. Both giving and receiving feedback require skill, and skill requires practice.

sections.heading: Why feedback conversations fail
sections.text: Difficult conversations fail for a small number of predictable reasons. The most common is that the person giving feedback conflates the observable behaviour with a judgment about the other person's character or intent. "You were late to three meetings" is an observation; "you don't respect other people's time" is an attribution of intent. Attributions trigger defensiveness immediately, because the other person experiences them — often correctly — as an unfair characterisation of who they are. A second common failure is timing. Feedback delivered in the heat of a moment, or in front of others, is almost never received well. When emotions are high, the receiver has tunnel vision rather than being able to calmly process what is being said. Equally, waiting too long is a problem — feedback loses specificity and usefulness as memory fades. The general principle is to wait until both parties are in a position to listen, be present, and discuss calmly, without waiting so long that the moment has passed. A third failure is the absence of an established relationship. When the person giving feedback has not built sufficient trust or credibility with the receiver, the feedback is likely to feel inappropriate regardless of its content. As a rule of thumb, feedback should not be given when it has not been asked for and the relationship does not yet support it. When in doubt, ask the other person whether they are open to hearing your perspective before offering it. A fourth failure is the absence of specificity. Vague feedback ("you need to communicate better") gives the receiver nothing to act on, and often reads as a verdict rather than a direction. Specific, behavioural feedback gives someone something concrete to engage with.

sections.heading: The SARA model: understanding the emotional arc
sections.text: When someone receives feedback that is critical, challenging, or unexpected, they typically move through a predictable emotional sequence before they are able to genuinely engage with the content. This sequence is described by the SARA model. Knowing the model is useful in both directions — as a receiver it helps you name what you are experiencing; as a giver it helps you not mistake early-stage reactions for final responses. Surprise is the first response to unexpected feedback. The person is caught off guard. Even if the feedback is accurate and well-delivered, the initial response is often a kind of defensiveness or disconnection. Nothing much can be processed at this stage. Anger follows when the surprise resolves into a reactive emotion. The person may feel attacked, misunderstood, or treated unfairly. They are likely to push back, deflect, or look for flaws in the feedback. This is not bad faith — it is a normal defensive response to perceived threat. Resistance is the stage where the person actively pushes back against the feedback to protect their self-image. They may make excuses, question the validity of the data or the person giving it, or agree outwardly without any genuine intention to change. This is the hardest stage to move past, because it requires accepting a truth that is uncomfortable. It often happens away from the original conversation — after sleeping on it — and may not be visible to the feedback giver at all. Acceptance is the stage where the person is able to see the feedback with some objectivity and make a choice: to act on it, or to reject it. This is the only stage at which genuine learning and change become possible. Importantly, acceptance is a choice — not all feedback deserves to be acted on, and the receiver should carefully consider what they take on board and what they set aside. The practical implication of the SARA model is that feedback conversations are almost never resolved in a single exchange. A person who leaves a difficult conversation in the Anger or Resistance stage has not permanently rejected the feedback — they may simply need time and space to move through the arc. Following up a day or two later often produces a very different conversation. How to use SARA when receiving feedback. The most powerful aspect of the model is recognising that moving through these stages is a normal human reaction, not a personal failing. When you receive tough feedback and notice shock, anger, or the urge to resist, name the stage to yourself: "I'm in the Anger stage — I don't need to respond right now." Avoid reacting immediately while in the Surprise, Anger, or Resistance stages — your judgment will be clouded and a defensive response rarely serves you. A simple "Thank you for the feedback, I need some time to think about it" is a legitimate and often ideal response. When you have moved past the strongest emotions, return to the feedback and listen with the goal of understanding rather than defending. And allow yourself time — do not try to force yourself to Acceptance immediately.

sections.heading: Non-violent communication
sections.text: Non-violent communication (NVC) is a structured approach to interpersonal communication developed by Marshall Rosenberg. It is designed to keep conversations focused on concrete reality and genuine needs, rather than on evaluations, judgments, and demands. In organisational settings, it is particularly useful in feedback and conflict conversations where there is already some emotional charge. NVC organises communication around four elements, always in this sequence. Observations are specific, factual descriptions of what happened, stripped of evaluation. The test is whether a camera could have captured it. "In the last three planning sessions, you arrived more than ten minutes after the start time" is an observation. "You're always late" is a judgment dressed as an observation. The distinction matters enormously, because evaluations invite argument while observations invite engagement. In escalated conflicts in particular, people tend to confuse facts, opinions, prejudices, and feelings. Separating these out is difficult but vital. Feelings are the emotional response that the observation triggered in you. NVC distinguishes carefully between feelings and interpretations. "I feel ignored" is actually an interpretation — it contains a theory about what the other person intended. "I feel frustrated" or "I feel anxious about our shared deadlines" is a genuine feeling statement. Feelings are not signs that something is right or wrong — they are neutral data that point toward unmet needs. Being transparent about feelings and demonstrating some vulnerability, though uncomfortable, is key to building the kind of understanding that makes resolution possible. Needs are the underlying values or requirements that your feelings are pointing to. The cause of our feelings can generally be tied to needs that have not been met or have been violated — the need to be accepted, trusted, respected, or recognised, among many others. When it is clear which needs have been neglected, it becomes possible to examine how to fulfil those needs and, thus, move toward resolution. Naming the need rather than continuing to focus on the behaviour shifts the conversation from blame to understanding. Requests are specific, concrete, and positive — they describe an action you are asking for, not a behaviour you want to stop. "Would you be willing to message the group by 8:45 if you know you'll be delayed?" is a request. "Stop being late" is a demand. While demands create a power struggle with only submission or rebellion as options, requests are concrete suggestions for future interaction. They give the other party something they can do to help improve the situation and build trust. Requests invite agency; demands generate compliance or resistance. In practice, you do not need to use NVC as a rigid script. The four-element structure is most useful as a preparation tool: before a difficult conversation, work through what the observations actually are, what you genuinely feel, what need is underneath that feeling, and what specific change you are asking for. That preparation alone will significantly improve the quality of the conversation you actually have.

sections.heading: Structuring a feedback conversation
sections.text: A practical structure for a difficult feedback conversation in a professional context has five phases. Opening sets the intention. Be direct about the purpose of the conversation without being aggressive. "I want to talk about something that's been creating friction for me, and I'd like us to find a way through it together" is an honest opening that signals partnership rather than accusation. Observation shares the specific behaviour you observed, using the NVC distinction between fact and evaluation. Stay with what you saw or experienced — do not venture into what you think it means about the person. Impact shares the effect the behaviour had — on you, on the team, on the work. This is not blame; it is information. Many people are genuinely unaware of the downstream effects of their behaviour. Sharing impact without attributing intent gives the other person something to engage with rather than defend against. Inquiry asks a genuine question before moving to requests or solutions. "What was going on for you in those meetings?" or "Is there something I'm not seeing from your side?" This is not a rhetorical move — it is an acknowledgment that you may have an incomplete picture, and that the other person's perspective is relevant to finding a workable solution. Forward movement — only once the other person has had space to respond — is where you make a specific, actionable request. If the conversation has gone well, this often becomes a collaborative problem-solving moment rather than a unilateral demand.

sections.heading: The VIBE framework: observing what is really being communicated
sections.text: One of the most common failure modes in feedback and difficult conversations is taking what someone says at face value while missing what they are actually communicating. People do not always express their real concerns directly — sometimes because they are not fully aware of them, and sometimes because the social context makes it difficult. The VIBE framework is a practical tool for observing the consistency between what someone says and how they say it, across four simultaneous channels. Voice covers paraverbal communication — not the words themselves, but the tone, volume, speaking speed, and pauses. A voice that trembles, accelerates, or goes flat can signal tension, uncertainty, or disengagement even when the words express the opposite. Information is the verbal content: the facts, data, and logic of what is being said. This is the "what." The observer notes whether the information is clear, vague, or internally contradictory — and whether it is consistent with what was said previously. Body language is the non-verbal channel: posture, gestures, facial expressions, and eye contact. The body often communicates what the mind is trying to conceal. Someone claiming openness while sitting with crossed arms and avoiding eye contact is sending two different signals simultaneously. Emotions is the overall energy or climate the person is emanating — the underlying emotional tone that colours the entire interaction. It is the synthesis of how the other three channels combine. A person might describe a situation using neutral words, but the emotional atmosphere they create might be one of anxiety, frustration, or resignation. The main practical value of VIBE is identifying inconsistencies. If the information is positive ("I'm fine with this decision") but the voice is flat and the body language is withdrawn, the perceived emotion tells a different story. Noticing these discrepancies gives you the opportunity to ask a more targeted question rather than accepting a surface-level answer and moving on — which often means the real issue stays unaddressed.

sections.heading: Receiving feedback
sections.text: Constructive disagreement is not only a skill for the person giving feedback. Receiving feedback well — especially unexpected or critical feedback — is equally important and equally learnable. The most important practice is to delay evaluation. When you receive feedback that stings or surprises you, resist the immediate impulse to agree, disagree, or explain. Simply listen and ask clarifying questions. "Can you say more about what you observed?" or "When specifically did that happen?" are not defensive moves — they are ways of gathering information before you respond. It also helps to proactively seek feedback from people whose opinion you respect, about specific behaviours or aspects of your work that you want to improve. Being proactive reduces the sense of surprise, and choosing trusted people reduces the anger response. Requesting feedback in advance also allows the giver to formulate their observations carefully, rather than relying on an imprecise recollection. Remember that not all feedback deserves to be accepted. Consider carefully what you take on board and what you set aside. And when someone takes the time and courage to give you feedback — thank them for it, regardless of whether you agree.

resources.title: Decision Latency and Flow Diagnosis
resources.summary: What decision latency is, why it matters, and the structural patterns that cause it most often. Value stream analysis as a diagnostic tool for knowledge work: how to build a flow diagram, what it reveals, and how it connects to decision protocol design.

sections.heading: What this resource is for
sections.text: AI accelerates delivery at the individual level. It does not automatically accelerate the decision-making, review, and coordination that surrounds that delivery. The result is a widening gap: teams can produce output faster than ever, but that output still needs to be reviewed, approved, prioritised, and integrated with the work of other teams. In many organisations, the decision-making processes that govern this work have not been updated to match the new tempo. Decision latency — the time between when a decision is needed and when it is made — has become one of the most significant constraints on actual delivery throughput. In AI-accelerated organisations, the bottleneck to delivery is rarely technical capability. Teams can produce output faster than ever — but that output still needs to be reviewed, approved, prioritised, and coordinated with other teams. The decision-making processes that surround the work are often dramatically slower than the work itself. This resource covers two related diagnostic tools: decision latency analysis, which identifies where decisions are slowing throughput, and value stream mapping, which provides the broader organisational view in which decision bottlenecks become visible.

sections.heading: Decision latency: the invisible tax on speed
sections.text: Decision latency is the elapsed time between when a decision is needed and when it is made. It is one of the most underappreciated sources of delivery slowdown, because it is often invisible in standard project tracking. A task may be "in progress" for three weeks, but if you examine the timeline carefully, two of those weeks were spent waiting — for approval, for a missing stakeholder to weigh in, for a meeting that finally happened, for clarity on a dependency. Decision latency compounds in complex organisations. A single delayed decision can block multiple downstream teams simultaneously, and the cost of that delay multiplies across everyone waiting. In an AI-accelerated environment, where the tempo of production has increased but governance structures have not been updated to match, decision latency is frequently the dominant constraint on actual delivery throughput. Three structural patterns account for most decision latency in practice. Centralised authority with distributed execution is the most common pattern. Decisions are made at a level of the organisation that is several steps removed from where the work happens. The people doing the work understand the problem deeply and could make a good decision quickly, but they are required to escalate. Each escalation step adds latency, introduces communication loss, and often produces a decision made by someone with less context. Missing decision owners occur when no one is clearly accountable for a decision. In organisations with highly collaborative or consensus-oriented cultures, this is surprisingly common. The decision gets discussed in meetings, passes through inboxes, and is referenced in documents — but because no one is explicitly responsible for making it, it drifts. Everyone assumes someone else will close it. Unclear decision criteria occur when people are not sure what counts as a good enough answer. Without clear criteria, reviews become open-ended, stakeholders feel entitled to relitigate settled questions, and decisions never quite reach closure.

sections.heading: Diagnosing decision latency
sections.text: A decision latency diagnosis examines a recent delivery cycle and asks specific questions about each decision point encountered. For each significant decision in the period under review, identify: when the need for the decision became apparent; when the decision was actually made; who made it; who was consulted; and whether the outcome was later reversed or relitigated. The gap between the first and second items is your latency figure. The other data points tell you what caused it. Look for patterns. If most delayed decisions share a common decision-maker, the bottleneck is a person (or a role), and the structural solution is either delegation or a clearer mandate. If most delayed decisions involve cross-team coordination, the bottleneck is a missing forum or protocol. If decisions are frequently relitigated after being made, the bottleneck is in how decisions are documented and communicated. The goal of the diagnosis is not to assign blame but to produce a structural map of where authority, accountability, and coordination are misaligned with the tempo of delivery.

sections.heading: Value stream mapping as a diagnostic lens
sections.text: Value stream mapping (VSM) is a lean practice originally developed for manufacturing, adapted widely for knowledge work. A value stream is the complete sequence of activities required to deliver value to a customer — from the moment a need is identified to the moment it is fulfilled. Mapping the value stream means making that sequence visible, including all the waiting, handoff, and rework that happens in between the productive steps. In knowledge work and software delivery, value stream maps typically reveal that a surprisingly small proportion of total elapsed time is actual productive work. The rest is waiting — for approvals, for dependencies, for capacity, for decisions. This ratio (value-adding time versus total elapsed time) is called the flow efficiency or process cycle efficiency, and it is frequently under 20% even in well-run organisations. In organisations with significant decision latency, it can be under 5%.

sections.heading: How to build a value stream map
sections.text: A value stream map for a delivery flow typically covers the following elements. Work stages are the discrete steps that a unit of work passes through from inception to delivery. In a software team, this might include: idea or request intake, refinement, development, code review, testing, deployment, monitoring. Each stage is represented as a box. Handoffs are the transitions between stages. Each handoff is an opportunity for delay. Note who hands off to whom, and how the handoff is triggered. Many delays hide in handoffs that are assumed to be instantaneous but are actually batched or queued. Wait times are the elapsed time a unit of work spends sitting between stages, waiting for the next stage to pick it up. These are distinct from the time spent actively working on the item within a stage. Wait times are represented between the stage boxes and are almost always larger than people expect. Process times are the time spent actively working on the item within each stage. Decision points are moments where a human judgment is required before the work can proceed. These may be explicit (a formal approval gate) or implicit (a developer waiting for a colleague to clarify a requirement before continuing). Once the map is built, the diagnostic questions become: where is most of the elapsed time being spent? Are the long waits in work stages or between them? Which decision points have the highest latency? What would need to change to halve the total elapsed time?

sections.heading: Connecting VSM to decision protocol design
sections.text: Value stream mapping is a powerful setup for decision protocol design because it makes the cost of poor decision-making visible in concrete terms. A decision that takes two weeks to reach closure is not an abstract governance problem — it is a visible delay in the map, with a calculable impact on throughput and customer value. When participants map their own value streams and identify decision bottlenecks, the conversation about decision protocols becomes practical rather than theoretical. The question shifts from "what is best practice for decision-making?" to "what needs to be true about how we make decisions here in order to remove this specific delay?" This is the frame for the decision protocol design work in the Decision-Making and Alignment module.

resources.title: The Cynefin Framework
resources.summary: The five domains of the Cynefin framework (Clear, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic, Confused), the decision process appropriate to each, and the failure modes that arise from domain confusion. Practical applications in planning, meeting facilitation, and escalation.

sections.heading: What this resource is for
sections.text: Not all decisions should be made the same way. A decision about which database engine to use is structurally different from a decision about how to enter a new market, which is structurally different from a decision about how to respond to an unexpected production incident. Applying the wrong decision process to a given situation creates real costs — either excessive slowness (running a consensus process on something that should be delegated) or dangerous confidence (applying a best-practice checklist to a situation that is fundamentally novel). The Cynefin framework is a sensemaking model that helps you match your decision process to the nature of the situation you are in.

sections.heading: The core idea: context determines method
sections.text: Cynefin (pronounced kuh-NEV-in, a Welsh word meaning "habitat" or "place of belonging") was developed by Dave Snowden, a Welsh management consultant and researcher. Its central claim is that situations differ in how cause and effect relate to each other, and that this difference should determine how you approach them. The framework divides situations into five domains, each with its own characteristics and corresponding approach for addressing problems.

sections.heading: The five domains
sections.text: Clear is the domain where the relationship between cause and effect is clear and obvious. There is an established best practice, and solutions are most reliably achieved by following standard operating procedures. This is the domain of known-knowns — what needs to be done is understood by anyone with appropriate training. The decision process is: sense what is happening, categorise it against known patterns, and respond with the established approach. Most routine operational decisions live here. The risk is complacency — over-categorising complex situations as clear because a familiar-looking pattern is present, or failing to notice when a previously stable situation has shifted. Complicated is the domain where the relationship between cause and effect is not immediately clear, and expertise is required to analyse and solve the problem. Solutions may require the involvement of subject matter experts, analytical tools, or established best practices — but the right answer can be found through analysis. This is the domain of known-unknowns: we know we don't know, and we know how to find out. The decision process is: sense what is happening, analyse it (usually with expert input), and respond with a considered approach. Engineering decisions, architectural trade-offs, and financial modelling typically live here. The risk is over-reliance on experts and the tendency to treat expertise as unquestionable. Complex is the domain where the relationship between cause and effect can only be understood in hindsight. The system is adaptive — it responds to interventions in ways that cannot be fully predicted in advance. This is the domain of unknown-unknowns: we don't know what we don't know, and analysis will not reveal the answer before we act. The decision process is different here: instead of analysing before acting, you run safe-to-fail experiments, observe the results, and amplify what works while dampening what does not. Product development, organisational change, and most strategic decisions in uncertain markets live here. The risk is trying to impose complicated-domain analysis on a complex situation — treating a living system like a machine. Chaotic is the domain where there is no discernible relationship between cause and effect, and the situation is rapidly changing. This is the domain of unknowables. Rapid decision-making and immediate action are necessary to bring stability to the situation — not analysis, not consultation. The decision process is: act first to reduce the chaos, sense what effects your actions are having, and respond by moving toward more stable ground. The risk is remaining in action mode after the crisis has stabilised, which prevents the reflection and learning that the situation requires. Confused is the domain in which it is unclear which of the other four domains applies. It is a state of confusion or uncertainty about the nature of the situation itself. The practical risk in confusion is that different people apply different frameworks simultaneously without realising it, leading to fragmented and contradictory responses. The goal when confused is to gather enough information to shift into one of the other four domains — to diagnose before deciding.

sections.heading: Why this matters for decision protocol design
sections.text: The most common failure mode in organisational decision-making is domain confusion. Teams apply best-practice thinking — the Clear domain approach — to situations that are actually Complex, because it feels more comfortable to follow a known process than to run experiments in uncertainty. Alternatively, teams that have learned to be adaptive in product development sometimes resist any process or structure, even when they are dealing with Complicated or Clear situations where structure would serve them well. A second common failure is expert overconfidence in Complicated domain situations. Having the right expert in the room is necessary but not sufficient — experts can be wrong, best practices can be outdated, and the analysis can miss important contextual factors. Good Complicated-domain decision-making includes challenge mechanisms and review alongside expert input. A third failure is the tendency to skip the Chaotic domain's act-first imperative. In a genuine crisis, attempting to run a structured analysis process before acting is itself a decision — usually the wrong one. Cynefin is explicit that speed of action takes priority over quality of analysis when the situation is genuinely chaotic. For decision protocol design, Cynefin gives you a diagnostic question to ask before choosing a process: what domain is this decision in? The answer determines whether you should be delegating to a trained operator, calling in an expert, running an experiment, or simply acting and observing.

sections.heading: Practical applications
sections.text: In a planning context, Cynefin helps teams avoid two opposite failure modes. Over-planning — writing detailed specifications for work that is actually in the Complex domain — generates waste because the system will not behave as predicted. Under-planning — treating genuinely Complicated technical problems as if they require experimentation rather than analysis — leads to avoidable rework that good upfront thinking would have prevented. In a meeting context, Cynefin helps facilitators recognise when a discussion is stuck because the group is applying the wrong mode of reasoning to the problem at hand. A group trying to analyse its way to a solution in a Complex domain situation will loop endlessly, because the analysis will not converge. The facilitator's intervention is to name the domain and propose a different approach — an experiment, a probe, a safe-to-fail pilot — rather than more analysis. In an escalation context, Cynefin helps clarify what you are actually asking when you escalate a decision . If the situation is Clear, escalation is probably waste — the answer is already known and someone closer to the work should apply it. If the situation is Complex, escalating to a senior decision-maker may actually reduce decision quality, because the senior person has less proximity to the signals that matter.

sections.heading: A note on boundaries
sections.text: The boundaries between domains in Cynefin are not fixed. Situations move. A situation that starts as Chaotic (an unexpected production outage) may stabilise into Complex (a systemic reliability problem requiring experimentation) and eventually into Complicated (a known class of failure with a recommended response). Tracking where a situation is in this arc, and adjusting your decision approach accordingly, is one of the most valuable skills that Cynefin develops. Snowden also warns specifically about the boundary between Clear and Chaotic — a boundary that can be crossed suddenly and without warning when an apparently stable situation collapses. Organisations that have been operating successfully in Clear-domain mode for a long time can be blindsided by conditions that invalidate their established practices overnight.

resources.title: Facilitating Convergence
resources.summary: The Diamond Model from Participatory Decision-Making: Business as Usual, the Divergent Zone, the Groan Zone, the Convergent Zone, and Closure. Consensus vs. consent-based closure. Types of powerful questions and how to sequence them to move groups from options to decisions.

sections.heading: What this resource is for
sections.text: In fast-moving organisations, the pressure to decide quickly is real — and the temptation to cut the decision process short is constant. AI-accelerated delivery creates conditions where alignment loops that used to take weeks now need to happen in hours. The risk is that groups skip the stages of a good decision process in the name of speed, and end up with decisions that unravel in implementation because the right perspectives were never heard. This resource covers how to move groups through a full decision process efficiently — creating genuine space for diverse perspectives while still reaching durable closure. Moving a group from a shared problem to a shared decision is one of the most demanding facilitation challenges in organisations. It requires creating genuine space for diverse perspectives while still reaching closure. Done poorly, it produces either shallow consensus (everyone agrees because no one felt safe to disagree) or endless divergence (every meeting produces more options and more questions, but no decisions). This resource covers the Diamond Model from Participatory Decision-Making — a structural map of how group decision processes work — and the role of powerful questions in guiding groups through that process.

sections.heading: What facilitation is
sections.text: Facilitation is the practice of helping a group identify shared objectives and move through a process to achieve them — while remaining neutral on the content. A facilitator does not decide what the group should conclude; they take responsibility for the quality of the process that leads to a conclusion. This distinction matters: when you step into the facilitator role, even temporarily, you set aside your own preferences about the outcome and focus entirely on enabling the group to think well together. Facilitation can be thought of in three phases. Before a session, the facilitator prepares: understanding the participants, designing the process, and clarifying the purpose. During the session, the facilitator is fully present — guiding without directing, holding the space without filling it. After the session, the facilitator follows up to ensure that agreements and decisions are carried forward into action. The facilitator's orientation throughout is toward three things: the purpose (what the group is trying to achieve), the people (ensuring everyone can participate and is heard), and the process (making sure the right things happen in the right order). When any of these three get neglected, the quality of the session suffers. Good facilitation requires a specific behavioural stance. The facilitator stays neutral and avoids expressing personal bias; remains curious and asks questions that open up multiple perspectives; is respectful of participants even when addressing difficult dynamics; and is observant — continuously reading the room for changes in energy, engagement, and tension. The facilitator also needs to be comfortable standing in the discomfort that often arises in good group work, rather than resolving it prematurely.

sections.heading: The Diamond Model
sections.text: The Diamond Model, developed by Sam Kaner and colleagues in Facilitator's Guide to Participatory Decision-Making, provides a structural description of how a group moves from a starting question to a decision. Understanding the model helps facilitators recognise where they are in the process and what kind of support the group needs at each stage. The model describes a shape comparable to a diamond. The group begins in a narrow starting zone, expands outward through divergence, passes through a wide and uncomfortable middle zone, then contracts inward through convergence, and arrives at a narrow closing zone — a decision. The model is not linear in practice, but it gives the facilitator a map of the territory and a language for naming where the group is at any given moment. A key insight from the model is that divergent thinking and convergent thinking cannot happen at the same time — they interfere with one another. The facilitator must make deliberate space for each stage at the appropriate moment.

sections.heading: The four zones
sections.text: Business as Usual is the starting point of most conversations. In this zone, team members do not challenge the status quo and tend toward obvious, familiar solutions to the problem. They refrain from taking risks or being ambitious. The group is operating within the boundaries of what is already known and accepted. The facilitator should pay attention to the quality and quantity of each person's contribution. If the team converges too quickly on a proposal without genuinely exploring the problem space, the facilitator can help them move into the divergent zone by opening up the question and inviting different perspectives. The Divergent Zone is where opinions and ideal solutions begin to differ. The atmosphere in this zone can be playful, curious, or nervous — creative thinking is happening, and not everyone is comfortable with it. This is the zone the facilitator must protect most carefully. Good divergence is genuinely inclusive: it surfaces viewpoints that would otherwise be suppressed, names concerns that would otherwise sabotage implementation later, and produces a richer solution space than any individual could have generated alone. The facilitator's job here is to hold the space open — using brainstorming, go-arounds, paraphrasing, and powerful questions to ensure that ideas are shared and diverse points of view are expressed without evaluation or pushback. Dissent must be protected in this zone; many great solutions start off as odd or seemingly silly ideas. The Groan Zone is the name Kaner gives to the middle section of the diamond — the widest, messiest, most uncomfortable part of the process. When team members have shared their divergent perspectives, conflicts begin to emerge. This feels uncomfortable and stressful. The temptation is to collapse back to a safe, familiar answer rather than sit with the complexity. But these conflicts also fuel progress — they force team members to search for ways to integrate their different views and build a more durable shared understanding. The groan zone is not a problem to be solved; it is a necessary phase to be navigated. When a team skips it, ideas are not understood well enough, and the result is premature convergence and a decision that will likely prove unsustainable. The facilitator's job here is to help team members understand each other's perspectives better by discussing ideas constructively, naming the discomfort explicitly ("this feeling of messiness is a sign we're doing it right"), and holding the space while integration happens. The Convergent Zone begins once the team has developed a shared enough understanding of the options on the table. Discussions feel smoother. There is a sense of making progress, and energy rises. The facilitator should let the team use this renewed energy to shortlist ideas and move toward a decision. Paraphrasing is helpful in this zone — reflecting back what has been said helps people recognise where they actually agree. Bridging questions are particularly valuable here: they sum up what has been heard and help build a figurative bridge between different positions, moving toward a conclusion the group can genuinely commit to.

sections.heading: Closure: reaching a decision
sections.text: The Closure Zone is where the group must decide on a way forward. The facilitator's job is to guide the team in making that decision while ensuring it is clear what it entails and that everyone's level of support is visible and explicit. A widespread confusion in organisational decision-making conflates consensus — everyone believes this is the best option — with consent-based closure — no one has a fundamental objection that would prevent moving forward. These are very different standards. Consensus is rare and often not worth pursuing. In most decisions, reasonable people with access to the same information will have different views. Requiring everyone to believe the chosen option is the best one before moving forward is a recipe for either endless process or manufactured agreement that masks real dissent. Consent-based closure asks a more tractable question: can you live with this decision and support its implementation, even if it is not your first choice? This is the right bar for most organisational decisions — it allows forward movement while respecting dissent. Participants who do not fully agree can still signal their support for moving forward, provided their core concerns have been heard and addressed. Techniques such as Fist-to-Five, the Decider Protocol, or explicit consent rounds make each team member's level of support visible. A clear signal that a group is ready to close is when no new substantive objections are being raised — when the conversation is recycling rather than generating. At that point, the facilitator calls for the closing gesture.

sections.heading: Practical techniques by zone
sections.text: Knowing which zone you are in is only useful if you have practical moves available for each. The following are not scripts — they are a repertoire to draw on as the situation requires. In the Divergent Zone , the facilitator's primary job is to protect the space from premature evaluation. Pause any criticism until brainstorming is genuinely complete. Use silent writing — asking participants to write ideas individually before sharing — so that quieter voices are not drowned out by more confident ones before they have formed their thoughts. Paraphrase what you hear to check understanding and signal that you are genuinely tracking what people say. Ask clarifying questions with phrases like "What I understand you're saying is..." or "Help me understand..." rather than evaluative ones. Occasional nods or short verbal cues ("and?", "tell me more") encourage the speaker without interrupting the flow. Mirror body language subtly to create rapport, or deliberately shift your own posture to change the energy when a discussion is getting stuck. In the Groan Zone , the facilitator's job is to hold the space rather than collapse it. Use structured go-arounds to ensure every voice is heard before the group moves on. Invite individual writing before wider sharing, which surfaces deeper reflections that might be lost in open discussion. Break into pairs or small groups to explore a specific tension in more depth and then report back to the whole group — this often unlocks perspectives that people are reluctant to voice in a larger setting. Resist the pull to resolve the discomfort too quickly; name it explicitly so the group understands that what they are feeling is a productive sign, not evidence of failure. In the Convergent Zone , the facilitator's job is to bring discipline to the closing. Make the available decision-making techniques visible — Fist-to-Five, majority vote, consent round, Decider Protocol — and explain them briefly so the group can choose consciously rather than defaulting to an implicit process. Check whether the group has an existing working agreement about how they make decisions; if not, facilitate a quick agreement before proceeding. Focus the group on committing to one or two concrete actions rather than an overwhelming list that dilutes accountability.

sections.heading: Diamonds within diamonds
sections.text: The Diamond Model does not only apply to entire meetings or workshops. It applies equally to individual segments within a longer session. Any time a group needs to explore a question, work through a disagreement, or arrive at a sub-decision, the same pattern applies: open the space, navigate the discomfort, close toward something concrete. Thinking in terms of nested diamonds — a large diamond for the overall session, with smaller diamonds within each major segment — helps the facilitator plan more precisely and recognise more quickly when a segment has become stuck. A divergence that is not producing new ideas is probably ready to move to the groan zone. A groan zone that is looping without integration is probably ready for a focused convergence move. The facilitator who can read these signals within a segment, not just across the whole session, will produce much tighter and more productive meetings.

sections.heading: Powerful questions
sections.text: Facilitation is, in large part, the art of asking the right question at the right moment. The questions a facilitator uses shape what the group is able to think about, and different types of questions serve different purposes across the zones. Opening questions are used to begin the divergent zone. They are designed to be genuinely generative — to invite multiple valid answers rather than converging on one. "What are all the factors we should consider before making this decision?" or "What would a successful outcome look like from each of your perspectives?" are opening questions. The test is whether the question invites one answer or many. Deepening questions develop and explore what has been offered. They follow something a participant has said and invite more. "Can you say more about that?" "What makes that the most important factor for you?" "What would we need to believe for that option to be the right choice?" Deepening questions signal that the facilitator is genuinely tracking the content, not just managing a process. Broadening questions surface perspectives that have not yet been heard. "Who hasn't spoken to this yet?" "Are there people outside this room whose perspective we need to consider?" "What's the view we haven't heard yet that might be important?" Broadening questions interrupt the tendency for discussions to be dominated by the most confident or senior voices. Bridging questions are particularly valuable in the convergent zone. They draw together what has been said and help the group move from a collection of positions toward something they can share. "Looking at everything on the table, what themes do we keep coming back to?" or "Where do we actually agree, even if we haven't said it explicitly?" are bridging questions. They build the connection between different contributions and help the group recognise its own emerging consensus. Convergence questions move the group toward integration and closure. "Of all the options on the table, which best addresses the concerns we've named?" "What would we need to agree on first in order to move forward?" "Is there a proposal here that you could all live with?" These questions are directive — they pull toward narrowing rather than expansion. Reality-check questions are used when the group is generating solutions without adequately engaging with constraints. "What would prevent this from working?" "What would need to be true for this to succeed?" "Who else would need to be on board for this to happen?" These catch problems in the convergence phase rather than after the decision has been implemented.

sections.heading: Sequencing in practice
sections.text: A common facilitation mistake is mixing divergence and convergence questions in an unstructured way, which produces a conversation that neither expands effectively nor closes. The facilitator loses track of where they are, the group loses coherence, and the meeting ends with a vague sense of discussion rather than a decision. The Diamond Model suggests a clearer sequencing. Begin in the Business as Usual zone and assess whether the group needs to be moved into genuine divergence. Use broadening and opening questions to expand the space. Hold the divergent zone with deepening questions and protect dissent. Navigate the groan zone by facilitating understanding across perspectives rather than pushing for premature resolution. Signal the transition to convergence explicitly — "We've heard a lot of important perspectives. I want to start moving toward what we can agree on." Then use bridging and convergence questions to close, and call for an explicit decision gesture in the closure zone. Groups move back and forth within the diamond, and sometimes a convergence attempt surfaces a new concern that requires revisiting the divergent zone. But the facilitator should always know which zone they are in and be deliberate about how they move between them.

resources.summary: Conway's Law as the foundational premise for team design. Principles for drawing good team boundaries: aligning to value streams, matching size to communication capacity, separating concerns by rate of change, and making ownership explicit. End-to-end, capability, and enabling team types and their trade-offs. How to surface dependencies between teams, read the patterns they reveal, and choose the right structural response.

concepts.name: Loosen, formalise or eliminate a dependency

sections.heading: What this resource is for
sections.text: How an organisation structures its teams determines, more than almost anything else, how information flows, how decisions get made, and how work reaches delivery. Teams that are structured poorly generate coordination cost, communication overhead, and delivery bottlenecks that no amount of process improvement can fully resolve. In AI-accelerated environments, where the tempo of output has increased but organisational structures were often designed for a slower pace, the mismatch between team design and delivery demand is one of the most significant — and most fixable — sources of friction. This resource covers two connected topics: how to think about team design as a deliberate act of organisational choice, and how to surface the dependencies between teams that reveal where the current structure is creating unnecessary cost.

sections.heading: Structure shapes communication and communication shapes the product
sections.text: The most important starting point for team design is Conway's Law, an observation made by computer scientist Melvin Conway in 1968: organisations tend to produce systems that mirror their own communication structures. If three teams are building a product together, the product will tend to develop three major components — not necessarily because that is the right architecture, but because each team builds what it can build independently and integrates at the points where it must communicate with others. Conway's Law is not a technical observation — it is an organisational one, and it applies far beyond software. The implication is significant in both directions. If you want to change how a system or product is structured, you often need to change how the teams building it are organised. And if you reorganise teams without thinking about the work they are trying to coordinate, the new structure will shape the work in ways you did not intend. The practical lesson is that team design is not primarily an HR or resource question — it is a product and delivery question. The boundaries you draw around teams determine what those teams can do independently and what they will need to negotiate with others. Drawing those boundaries well is one of the highest-leverage interventions available to a leader in a complex organisation.

sections.heading: What makes a team boundary good or bad
sections.text: A team boundary is the line that defines what a team owns and is accountable for. Good team boundaries share a few properties. A good boundary encloses a coherent domain of work. The things inside the boundary belong together — they change together, they are understood together, and they are best decided on together. When a boundary cuts across a naturally coherent domain, the two teams on either side will need to coordinate constantly on things that should be internal decisions. This coordination is not free — it consumes time, introduces latency, and creates opportunities for misalignment. A good boundary minimises mandatory coordination. Every time one team needs something from another team in order to proceed, a dependency exists. Dependencies are not inherently bad, but every dependency is a potential bottleneck. A team that can complete most of its important work without waiting for other teams will deliver faster and more predictably than one that is constantly blocked on others. The goal of boundary design is to make the most frequent and most critical work as independent as possible, pushing coordination needs toward the edges. A good boundary comes with clear ownership. The team on the inside of the boundary is accountable for what happens there. They make the decisions, they bear the consequences, and they do not need to seek approval from outside for routine choices within their domain. Boundary ambiguity — areas where two teams both believe, or neither believes, they are responsible — is one of the most common sources of both conflict and delivery failure .

sections.heading: Principles for designing team structures
sections.text: Several principles from organisational design research are durable and well-supported, regardless of the specific framework you apply them through. Align teams to value streams, not functions. A value stream is the sequence of activities required to deliver something of value to a user or customer. When teams are aligned to value streams — owning an end-to-end capability — they can make decisions and deliver independently. When teams are aligned to functions — one team for design, one for engineering, one for testing — every feature requires multiple teams to coordinate, and the organisational structure itself becomes a bottleneck. Functional structures are good at building deep expertise; they are poor at delivering integrated value quickly. Match team size to communication capacity. There is a well-established relationship between team size and communication overhead. As team size grows, the number of communication channels grows faster — a team of five has ten possible communication pairs; a team of ten has forty-five. This is not just a theoretical concern: empirically, small teams communicate more effectively, make faster decisions, and maintain shared context more reliably than large ones. The commonly cited range of five to nine people for a working team is grounded in this reality, not arbitrary convention. Separate concerns at different rates of change. Some parts of a system or product change frequently; others change rarely. When fast-changing and slow-changing concerns are owned by the same team, the team's rhythm is determined by the fastest-changing element — which may not be appropriate for everything it owns. Separating concerns by rate of change allows each team to operate at a pace that matches its domain. Make ownership explicit and complete. Every significant capability, system component, or customer-facing outcome should have a clear owning team. Gaps in ownership — things that everyone assumes someone else is responsible for — reliably produce delivery failures and escalating conflicts. A complete ownership map, even a rough one, is more valuable than a sophisticated organisational chart that leaves accountability implicit.

sections.heading: Team types and their trade-offs
sections.text: While no single framework has a monopoly on how to categorise teams, a few recurring distinctions are worth understanding because they reflect real structural trade-offs. End-to-end teams own a complete user journey or customer capability from interface to infrastructure. They are responsible for outcomes, not just outputs — for whether the user can successfully do something, not just for whether a component was built. End-to-end ownership maximises accountability and minimises handoffs, but it requires breadth of skill within the team and can create tension when a technical component is shared across multiple journeys. Capability or platform teams provide shared services or infrastructure that other teams consume. Rather than building every team's own solution to a common problem, a capability team builds it once and makes it available. This pattern is efficient when the shared capability is genuinely common and stable — but it creates a dependency for every team that relies on it. A slow, unreliable, or unresponsive capability team becomes a bottleneck for everyone downstream. Enabling or coaching teams are temporary structures whose purpose is to build capability in other teams — not to do work on their behalf. An enabling team works alongside other teams for a defined period, transfers knowledge and practice, and then moves on. The measure of their success is whether the teams they worked with no longer need them. The most important question when choosing a team type is not which pattern is theoretically best but which best minimises the coordination cost for the most important work in your specific context. There is no universally correct answer, and the right structure for a fifty-person organisation is almost certainly wrong for a five-hundred-person one.

sections.heading: Dependency discovery
sections.text: Dependencies between teams are one of the most significant and most underexamined sources of delivery slowdown. A dependency exists whenever one team cannot complete meaningful work without something from another team. Dependencies are not inherently bad — in any organisation where teams specialise, some dependencies are inevitable. But unexamined dependencies create invisible bottlenecks, unpredictable delivery timelines, and recurring friction between teams that each believe the other is the problem. Dependency discovery is the practice of making these dependencies visible before they become crises. It is most valuable at the start of a delivery cycle or planning period, when there is still time to act on what is found. What to look for. Dependencies fall into a few recurring categories. Technical dependencies arise when one team's system or output is an input to another team's work. Knowledge dependencies arise when one team needs expertise or context that lives in another team. Approval dependencies arise when one team requires sign-off from another team or function before proceeding. Resource dependencies arise when teams share access to people, infrastructure, or tooling that is finite. How to surface them. The most reliable method is a structured conversation, not a survey. Bring team representatives together and ask, for each significant piece of planned work: what do we need from other teams that we cannot provide ourselves? What other teams need something from us that would block them if we were delayed? These questions surface both outgoing and incoming dependencies — both matter. For each dependency identified, note: which teams are involved; what specifically is needed; how frequently this dependency arises; how critical it is (does it block delivery, or just slow it?); and whether there is currently a clear protocol for managing it. Reading the map . Once dependencies are visible, patterns become apparent. Concentration is the most important pattern to look for: if one team or component appears as a dependency for many other teams, it is a structural bottleneck. Any delay, instability, or capacity constraint in that team propagates across everyone who depends on it. Circular dependencies — where Team A needs something from Team B, and Team B needs something back from Team A — are a second critical pattern. Circular dependencies can create mutual blockages that neither team can resolve independently. Acting on what you find. There are three structural responses to a problematic dependency. You can loosen it by building the needed capability into the dependent team , so they no longer need to wait. You can formalise it by putting a clear interface, agreement, or service commitment in place — converting an ad-hoc coordination need into a predictable relationship. Or you can eliminate it by redesigning team ownership so that the things that need to go together are owned by the same team. The right response depends on the nature of the dependency, the frequency and criticality of the need, and what is feasible given the current structure and skills.

sections.heading: The connection to coordination patterns
sections.text: Dependency discovery is not an end in itself — it is the input to coordination design. Once you know what your dependencies are, the question becomes: what is the right mechanism for managing each one? That question is covered in Resource 08 — Coordination Patterns and Flight Levels , which maps specific coordination approaches to specific dependency types and organisational contexts.
